state.misconception_label: Believes f(x - a) translates the function up a units

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: What transformation maps the graph of \(y=f(x) \) to the graph of \( y=f(x-3) \). I got Translation by vector
\(
\left[\begin{array}{l}
0 \\
3
\end{array}\right]
\) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you walk me through your thought process on how you arrived at the translation vector \(\left[\begin{array}{l} 0 \\ 3 \end{array}\right]\)? Let's delve deeper into why you chose those specific values for the transformation.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Well, I thought that since the \(x\) value is being subtracted by 3 in \(f(x-3)\), it would mean the graph moves up by 3 units. I guess I mixed up the directions for the transformations. So, does that mean it actually moves to the right instead? I'm a bit confused about how the subtraction affects the graph.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you think of any other ways in which subtracting 3 from the input might affect the graph? How does this relate to the misconception that shifting by \(a\) units always means moving up or down?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher asks vague, open-ended questions that don't directly address the vertical vs. horizontal confusion, and while the student identifies their confusion in Turn 2, Turn 3 fails to provide clear guidance, leaving the misconception unresolved.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses probing questions to guide the student's thinking and attempts to expose the flawed reasoning about direction of transformation, though they stop short of providing a concrete counterexample that would make this a perfect exemplar.
